name: Will Brown
bio: Will Brown leads Applied Research at Prime Intellect and builds open research infrastructure to enable every company to train, deploy, and self-improve their own frontier agentic models. He holds a PhD in Computer Science from Columbia University.

positions.claim: Environments and evals are the same unit of logic, so building evals is a prerequisite for and on-ramp to post-training rather than a separate track.
Synchronous RL training is the wrong choice; the off-policyness of async is worth accepting because agent rollouts have long tails.
Running roughly 16 steps off-policy on average is empirically fine for RL stability.
SFT data pipelines that export, reformat, and re-upload datasets are unnecessary — SFT is just rollouts in an environment where the actor is a teacher.
Frontier-scale RL is now economically accessible to enterprises: ~$50K buys a 1,000-step GLM-5 run on real agentic coding tasks, comparable to a month of token spend.
Torch Titan is a better base for a hackable training framework than Megatron.
Chat templates and Jinja are a significant source of trainer/inference mismatch, and replacing them with programmable renderers is necessary for stable large-scale runs.
Stateful LLM APIs like OpenAI's Responses API were the right call, because agentic rollouts make token-level state management unavoidable.
Training multiple RL experts on a shared base model and distilling them into one checkpoint is more reliable than training a single model on many environments at once.
Models will grow their chains of thought without bound unless reward design actively counteracts it.
Coupling training, inference, and environments into one stack is a design mistake because it prevents using environments as standalone evals.
The right architecture keeps harness code ignorant of RL entirely, so the same harness runs in training and production.
Environments and evals are the same objects, and one environment can serve RL, SFT data generation, on-policy distillation, and prompt optimization.
Most real-world agent tasks are not verifiable; verifiable rewards (math answers, code tests, database state) are the easy special case.
Handcrafted benchmarks of a few hundred expert-built tasks are not a scalable basis for training on open-ended real-world work.
Generalizing outside the training distribution is an undefined problem in classical ML terms, so the distribution must be discovered from deployment rather than specified up front.
Reward hacking arises specifically from proxies that are undefined at the boundaries, and models trained with RL will find those weaknesses.
The current level of abstraction for continual learning is too low to be practical for most practitioners, and most of the difficult steps are in fact automatable.
RL is effective at refining existing skills but poor at incorporating dense new knowledge into the model.
Deployed production traces are the best available source material for constructing tasks when no labels exist.
Working backwards from a known-reachable end state yields supervision for free and applies well beyond code.
Learned simulators are better RL environments than real production systems because full back-end controllability lets you plant answers and guarantee solvability.
Judging in hindsight — after seeing the full chain of events, or by polling several models — is more reliable than judging or instructing against failures in advance.
RL requires tasks calibrated to intermediate difficulty, because the advantage signal depends on separation across a set of rollouts.
Simple hindsight review catches most reward hacks in practice, whereas telling a judge model not to allow a behavior does not prevent it in the rollout.
Small training runs must be part of environment design because some problems only appear once RL is actually running.
Humans should be reserved for the highest-level judgments about goals and quality, with compute handling the rest of environment refinement.
An online loop of generating, solving, and synthesizing tasks gated on pass rate produced a large uplift on popular tool-use benchmarks.
Supervised learning signal from the environment gives the model a likelihood model of environment tokens — a native world model — which RL alone would not produce.
Environment and reward design will follow coding agents up the abstraction ladder, becoming largely automated.
